fixes.explanation: Samaria is a real place (1 Kings 16:24), but it never shows up in this story. The text says the vessels came from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem (Daniel 5:3). Mixing them up is like grabbing the wrong set of keys on the way out the door. Happens to the best of us, and I once spent an hour looking for a spatula I was holding.

Melting them down would be a plan, but it's not THIS plan. The text says Belshazzar, king of Babylon, wanted the vessels so that the king could drink from them with his nobles, his wives and his concubines. He gave that order under the influence of the wine. The vessels were headed for the cups.

It's actually True, friend. The text says that as they drank the wine, “…they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.” That's the list: six materials, and those gods were made from them. Belshazzar and his guests were doing this while drinking from vessels taken from God's house.

Yes! The text says “…his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.” A moment ago, Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was drinking wine with his nobles. Then the fingers of a hand started writing on his wall, and his knees did the knocking.

No cup raised toward that hand, friend. The text says his face grew pale and his knees knocked together. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was drinking wine a moment ago. Now it's his knees doing the talking.

Shouting for guards isn't what the text says. It says his face grew pale, his hips gave way and his knees knocked together. He does call out, but it's for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners (Daniel 5:7), not for guards. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was shaking before he called for anyone.

The elders of Israel aren't in this room, friend. The text says Belshazzar, Babylon's king, called for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners, “…these wise men of Babylon…” Those are the ones he sent for. Somebody will have to speak up for him.

Close, but the text says they couldn't do either one. The wise men “…could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” They could not read it, and they could not interpret it. The king's whole team of experts hit a wall, and I mean that literally.

That would be a neat trick, friend, explaining something you can't even read. The text says the wise men “…could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” They came up empty on both. That includes the reading.

That's right, False. The text says that after the wise men came up empty, “…King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.” He was already scared, and now he's scared on top of scared. His nobles were bewildered right along with him.

Yes! The queen says, “Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.” Nebuchadnezzar is Belshazzar's father, the king who took the temple vessels. She reminds Belshazzar that his own father was the one who appointed this man.

That's what she says. The queen tells him, “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” The room is full of outcry, and she walks in with one name. I think that's one calm queen.

The wise men already came in and couldn't help (Daniel 5:8). The queen sends Belshazzar a different direction: “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” She says this about one man, and she doesn't suggest bringing more experts.

That's right. Daniel tells Belshazzar, “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.” Belshazzar knew his father's story, and he still didn't humble his heart.

Daniel says nothing like that. He calls those gods ones that “…cannot see or hear or understand.” Then he says Belshazzar failed to glorify “…the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.” That's the God Daniel is talking about.

It's actually False. Daniel says to Belshazzar, “Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.” The “He” is the Lord of heaven, the God Belshazzar didn't glorify (Daniel 5:23). Daniel calls the gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone gods that “…cannot see or hear or understand.”

Yes. Daniel says, “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.” Notice who's doing the counting: God. Daniel says it right to Belshazzar's face, and I think that takes nerve.

That's the word. Daniel says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” Belshazzar was weighed, and he came up short. Daniel read that word out right in front of the king.

Faithful would be a nicer word, but Daniel doesn't say it. He says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was weighed and came up short. That's the message Daniel read out.

Egypt didn't even make the guest list, friend. Daniel says, “PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” The Medes and Persians are the ones he names. Nobody from Egypt is mentioned.

Yes! The text says, “…Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” Belshazzar was slain that very night (Daniel 5:30). Daniel had read PERES as the kingdom divided and given over to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:28).

Hiram, king of Tyre, belongs to Solomon's day (1 Kings 5:1), not to this story. The text says, “…Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” Tyre never comes up here. Belshazzar was slain that very night, and then the text names Darius.
